phrases.translation: Ṣãd. By the Quran, full of reminders
phrases.explanation: Early readers differed over the opening letter, reading it as a command to measure deeds against the Quran, as a divine oath, or as a name of the Quran itself, which is then sworn by as a scripture full of reminders. The surah opens by swearing by the Quran and then naming the resistance it met. The surah keeps returning to the Quran as a reminder that people are responsible to weigh.

phrases.translation: ˹This is the truth,˺ yet the disbelievers are ˹entrenched˺ in arrogance and opposition
phrases.explanation: The verse sets the truth of the revelation against a stubborn pride that separates people from it, a self-conceit and rivalry that refuses to listen rather than a lack of evidence. Its first movement joins a claim about revelation to a description of those who reject it. Its questions are designed to be answered by the listeners themselves.

phrases.translation: ˹Imagine˺ how many peoples We destroyed before them,
phrases.explanation: The chapter opens by pointing to earlier communities that were destroyed, so the present deniers are not the first to hear a warning or the first to reject it. The chapter treats the denial of one God as the root of the objections that follow. The surah treats patience as the Prophet's task while God handles the outcome.

phrases.translation: and they cried out when it was too late to escape
phrases.explanation: Their cry came when escape was no longer possible, since the punishment left no time for return or recovery, a pattern held up as a warning to those who come later. The early objections are reported so that they can be answered rather than ignored. Its scenes of judgment reverse the worldly status people trusted in.

phrases.translation: Now, the pagans are astonished that a warner has come to them from among themselves.
phrases.explanation: Their surprise is that the messenger is one of their own people, a human neighbour rather than a distant or angelic figure, which they treat as a reason to reject him. The passage sets a pattern of warning, rejection, and consequence that the rest of the surah develops. The stories show that honour with God can survive a serious error.

phrases.translation: And the disbelievers say, “This is a magician, a total liar
phrases.explanation: They answer the warning by labelling the messenger a magician and a liar, turning a moral claim into an accusation about the messenger's honesty. The chiefs' words show how inherited worship can become a public campaign against a messenger. The surah asks readers to see their own choices in the stories of earlier peoples.

phrases.translation: Has he reduced ˹all˺ the gods to One God?
phrases.explanation: The objection is to the claim that worship belongs to one God alone, which they present as an absurd reduction of the many powers they had served. The chapter treats the Quran's reminders as the standard by which deeds are measured. Its closing words give the argument back to the One who sent the reminder.

phrases.translation: Indeed, this is something totally astonishing.”
phrases.explanation: Calling the message astonishing shows how far inherited ideas had moved from the plain claim of God's oneness, a reaction the surah repeatedly answers. Pride and separation are named together, since refusing the truth also divides a community. Its portraits of kingship stress service rather than privilege.

phrases.translation: The chiefs among them went forth saying, “Carry on, and stand firm in devotion to your gods.
phrases.explanation: The leaders urge one another to keep to their idols, treating persistence in inherited worship as a communal duty rather than examining the message. The destroyed peoples of the past are introduced as evidence for the present deniers. The text treats the abuse of authority as a failure of judgment with lasting effects.

phrases.translation: Certainly this is just a scheme ˹for power˺
phrases.explanation: They dismiss the call to one God as a plot to gain authority, attributing a political motive to a messenger who asked them for nothing. The opening dispute is about who has the right to speak for God. Pride is treated as the root of rejection, not a lack of evidence.

phrases.translation: We have never heard of this in the previous faith.
phrases.explanation: Their appeal to earlier religion is reported in two ways, either as the faith of their own tribe or as the faiths before them, and in both cases it is used to dismiss the message as new. The surah opens by swearing by the Quran and then naming the resistance it met. The text leaves room for uncertainty where the reports differ, rather than forcing one view.

phrases.translation: This is nothing but a fabrication
phrases.explanation: They call the revelation an invention, a charge the chapter answers by pointing to the Quran's reminders and to the fate of earlier deniers. Its first movement joins a claim about revelation to a description of those who reject it. Its warnings are addressed to people who already had access to guidance.

phrases.translation: Has the Reminder been revealed ˹only˺ to him out of ˹all of˺ us?”
phrases.explanation: The complaint is about who received the revelation, since they cannot accept that guidance should come to one person among them rather than to their chiefs. The chapter lists earlier peoples who denied their messengers and were destroyed. The chapter values a warning delivered plainly over a claim to special status.

phrases.translation: In fact, they are ˹only˺ in doubt of My ˹revealed˺ Reminder.
phrases.explanation: The real cause is named as doubt about the revelation itself, a suspicion of the message rather than a reasoned judgment about its content. The single blast is presented as the end of the delay the deniers relied on. The surah treats the Day of Reckoning as the answer to a creation without purpose.

phrases.translation: In fact, ˹they do so because˺ they have not yet tasted My punishment
phrases.explanation: Their boldness is explained by delay: because judgment has not yet arrived, they speak as though no consequence will follow. The sarcastic request to hasten punishment is treated as a serious mistake. The chapter shows that power belongs to God even when His servants appear weak.

phrases.translation: Or ˹is it because˺ they possess the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord
phrases.explanation: The question asks whether they control the stores of God's mercy, including the gift of prophecy, so that they could decide who should receive it. The passage moves from argument about revelation to a warning about its consequences. The surah keeps joining belief in one God with the way a person judges and acts.

phrases.translation: —the Almighty, the Giver ˹of all bounties˺
phrases.explanation: The divine titles answer the claim, since the One who is mighty and gives without limit is not answerable to those who question His choice. The surah insists that guidance belongs to God's gift rather than to human rank. Its final promise leaves the timing with God and the response with the listener.

phrases.translation: Or ˹is it because˺ the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and everything in between belongs to them?
phrases.explanation: A second question asks whether they own the dominion of the heavens and the earth, since only such ownership could justify their claim to dispose of revelation. The reports preserve more than one reading of these objections without hiding the disagreement. The surah asks its readers to measure their deeds against what God has revealed.

phrases.translation: Let them then climb their way ˹to heaven, if their claim is true˺
phrases.explanation: The challenge to climb to heaven uses the word for a means or rope, which early reports describe as the gates of heaven or as unseen pathways, and exposes the emptiness of their claim. The deniers' confidence is traced to the fact that judgment had not yet arrived. The surah treats revelation as a gift that no community can claim to control.

phrases.translation: This is just another ˹enemy˺ force bound for defeat out there
phrases.explanation: The verse dismisses the opposing groups as a single confederate force that will be routed, so their numbers and confidence do not change the outcome. The section treats the rejection of messengers as one repeated story across history. Its descriptions of the next life are meant to shape decisions in this one.

phrases.translation: Before them, the people of Noah denied ˹the truth˺,
phrases.explanation: Noah's people are named first in a list of earlier communities who rejected their messengers, setting a pattern the present deniers are repeating. This section answers objections about who received the revelation and who controls mercy. The chapter makes responsibility personal even when error was shared.

phrases.translation: as did ’Âd, Pharaoh of the mighty structures
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh is described as lord of the tent-pegs, explained either by his lofty buildings, by instruments of torture, or by pegs used in games, and the reports keep these views together. The questions about treasuries and dominion expose claims that cannot be supported. The surah treats mercy and justice as working together rather than against each other.

phrases.translation: Thamûd, the people of Lot, and the residents of the Forest.
phrases.explanation: Thamud, Lot's people, and the people of the thicket are added to the list, and the thicket is described as dense, intertwined trees. The chapter lists earlier peoples who denied their messengers and were destroyed. The chapter presents the Quran as blessing and warning at the same time.

phrases.translation: These were ˹all˺ enemy forces
phrases.explanation: Each of these communities is called an opposing force, united not by strength but by their shared resistance to the messengers sent to them. The single blast is presented as the end of the delay the deniers relied on. The text insists that turning away from a message is a choice with a cost.

phrases.translation: Each rejected their messenger, so My punishment was justified
phrases.explanation: The punishment is described as deserved rather than arbitrary, because every community had denied the messenger who came to it with warning. The sarcastic request to hasten punishment is treated as a serious mistake. The chapter shows that those who lead others astray do not escape what follows.

phrases.translation: These ˹pagans˺ are awaiting nothing but a single Blast that cannot be stopped
phrases.explanation: What they await is one overpowering blast, understood as a destroying punishment from which there is no recovery, and the variant readings of the word do not change that meaning. The passage moves from argument about revelation to a warning about its consequences. Its contrasts are meant to be weighed, not merely admired.

phrases.translation: They say ˹mockingly˺, “Our Lord! Hasten for us our share ˹of the punishment˺ before the Day of Reckoning.”
phrases.explanation: Their demand to hasten their portion is reported in two ways, either as a challenge to bring on the punishment or as a sarcastic request for the promised reward, and the word for portion means a written allotment. The surah insists that guidance belongs to God's gift rather than to human rank. The chapter joins a warning about judgment to an invitation to turn back.

phrases.translation: Be patient ˹O Prophet˺ with what they say.
phrases.explanation: The command to patience comes directly after the mockery, telling the Prophet to bear their words without abandoning the message or answering in kind. The Quran is described as blessed so that people reflect on its verses. Every narrative in the surah points back to the oneness of God and the certainty of judgment.

phrases.translation: And remember Our servant, David, the man of strength.
phrases.explanation: David is introduced as a servant endowed with strength, a quality the reports connect with power in worship and obedience, and his story becomes a model for endurance. David's prostration shows that greatness does not remove the need for repentance. The chapter shows that delay in punishment is not the same as safety.

phrases.translation: Indeed, he ˹constantly˺ turned ˹to Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The description of him as constantly turning back to God frames the story that follows, so his kingship is read through repentance rather than through power alone. The passage moves from a private test to a public standard for those who judge. Gratitude appears as the proper response to a gift no one could earn.

phrases.translation: We truly subjected the mountains to hymn ˹Our praises˺ along with him in the evening and after sunrise
phrases.explanation: The mountains are said to join David's praise, and the reports say they proclaimed glorification with him at evening and after sunrise, so creation itself echoes his worship. David's story is told as a model of strength joined to repentance. Its questions about who controls mercy expose the limits of human authority.

phrases.translation: And ˹We subjected˺ the birds, flocking together.
phrases.explanation: The birds are gathered to him in flocks, another part of creation placed at his service for the praise of God. The chapter links his worship to the praise of the mountains and birds. The text treats every messenger's rejection as part of one long history.

phrases.translation: All turned to him ˹echoing his hymns˺
phrases.explanation: They are described as turning back to him, and one report broadens the meaning to say that everything glorifies God, with David's hymn at the centre. His kingship is described through justice, wisdom, and decisive judgment. The stories move quickly, but each one leaves a clear moral point.

phrases.translation: We strengthened his kingship, and gave him wisdom and sound judgment
phrases.explanation: His rule was strengthened, and he was given wisdom and decisive judgment, understood as knowledge of prophetic practice, as the rule that a claimant must bring proof while the defendant swears an oath, or as awe in the people's eyes. The story of the two plaintiffs is told as a test rather than as a legal report alone. The text gives space to doubt so that it can be answered rather than hidden.

phrases.translation: Has the story of the two plaintiffs, who scaled the ˹wall of David’s˺ sanctuary, reached you ˹O Prophet˺
phrases.explanation: The story of the two disputants who climbed into David's private sanctuary is introduced as a test, and reports describe them as two angels who appeared in human form. The chapter turns a court case into a lesson about a prophet's self-examination. Its closing reminder answers the opening oath by the same Quran.

phrases.translation: When they came into David’s presence, he was startled by them.
phrases.explanation: David is startled by their sudden appearance in a place he thought secure, which is why they immediately tell him not to be afraid. The command to judge with truth stands at the centre of this passage. The fate of earlier peoples is offered as a pattern the present deniers are repeating.

phrases.translation: They said, “Have no fear. ˹We are merely˺ two in a dispute: one of us has wronged the other.
phrases.explanation: They present themselves as two parties in a genuine dispute, one having wronged the other, and the word for disputants is singular in form though plural in meaning. The section connects the purpose of creation to the reality of a final judgment. The chapter treats justice in judgment as a duty laid on those who hold authority.

phrases.translation: So judge between us with truth—do not go beyond ˹it˺—and guide us to the right way
phrases.explanation: They ask for a judgment based on truth without excess, meaning justice that does not overstep, and for guidance to the right way rather than a verdict that favours one side. The Quran is described as blessed so that people reflect on its verses. The text insists that inherited practice is not proof of truth.

phrases.translation: This is my brother. He has ninety-nine sheep while I have ˹only˺ one.
phrases.explanation: The complaint contrasts ninety-nine sheep with a single one, and one line of interpretation reads the sheep as wives, so the wrong is about taking a man's only wife. David's prostration shows that greatness does not remove the need for repentance. Its repeated command to remember makes reflection a duty, not a hobby.

phrases.translation: ˹Still˺ he asked me to give it up to him, overwhelming me with ˹his˺ argument.”
phrases.explanation: The stronger party is said to have overcome the weaker in argument, so the case turns on power used to pressure someone who has almost nothing. The passage moves from a private test to a public standard for those who judge. Its language of tasting, seeing, and knowing makes the consequences concrete.

phrases.translation: David ˹eventually˺ ruled, “He has definitely wronged you in demanding ˹to add˺ your sheep to his.
phrases.explanation: David gives judgment before hearing a defence, and the ruling concerns the wrong of demanding the one sheep to add to the ninety-nine. David's story is told as a model of strength joined to repentance. The surah treats the hastening of punishment as a reckless request, not courage.

phrases.translation: And certainly many partners wrong each other, except those who believe and do good—but how few are they!”
phrases.explanation: He adds that most partners wrong one another, with the exception of those who believe and do good, who are few, a comment the reports link to the case before him. The chapter links his worship to the praise of the mountains and birds. The text treats a prophet's honesty as central to the message he brings.

phrases.translation: Then David realized that We had tested him so he asked for his Lord’s forgiveness, fell down in prostration, and turned ˹to Him in repentance˺
phrases.explanation: David understands the case as a test from God and turns to Him in prostration and repentance, and reports differ over what brought the test about, including a request to be tried as earlier prophets were. His kingship is described through justice, wisdom, and decisive judgment. The surah honours obedience that does not wait for a guaranteed outcome.

phrases.translation: So We forgave that for him.
phrases.explanation: The response to his repentance is forgiveness, showing that the point of the test is restoration rather than disgrace. The story of the two plaintiffs is told as a test rather than as a legal report alone. Its stories are told as signs for the listener, not only as records of the past.

phrases.translation: And he will indeed have ˹a status of˺ closeness to Us and an honourable destination
phrases.explanation: He is promised nearness to God and a good final home, so the story ends with honour rather than with the mistake that prompted it. The chapter turns a court case into a lesson about a prophet's self-examination. The chapter holds power and repentance together in its portraits of the prophets.

phrases.translation: ˹We instructed him:˺ “O David! We have surely made you an authority in the land, so judge between people with truth.
phrases.explanation: God addresses David as a vicegerent on earth after earlier messengers, and the command to judge with truth means with justice and equity. The command to judge with truth stands at the centre of this passage. The stories of David, Solomon, and Job share a single phrase about turning back to God.

phrases.translation: And do not follow ˹your˺ desires or they will lead you astray from Allah’s Way.
phrases.explanation: The warning is against letting inclination override justice in judgment, since desire would turn him away from the path God appointed for believers. The section connects the purpose of creation to the reality of a final judgment. The surah presents prophecy as one message delivered by many servants.

phrases.translation: Surely those who go astray from Allah’s Way will suffer a severe punishment for neglecting the Day of Reckoning.”
phrases.explanation: The reason given is forgetting the Day of Reckoning, because losing sight of accountability is what makes unjust judgment seem safe. The Quran is described as blessed so that people reflect on its verses. The chapter uses the failure of Iblis to show where pride leads.

phrases.translation: We have not created the heavens and earth and everything in between without purpose—as the disbelievers think.
phrases.explanation: The chapter rejects the idea that creation has no purpose, since the denial of a final judgment would make the whole order meaningless. David's prostration shows that greatness does not remove the need for repentance. Its arguments move from the visible world to truths that cannot be seen.

phrases.translation: So woe to the disbelievers because of the Fire
phrases.explanation: The warning of Fire follows from that denial, because a life lived without accountability ends in a loss its owners did not expect. The passage moves from a private test to a public standard for those who judge. The chapter treats reflection on the Quran as the purpose of its revelation.

phrases.translation: Or should We treat those who believe and do good like those who make mischief throughout the land?
phrases.explanation: The question assumes the answer is no, since a just God cannot reward obedience and corruption in the same way. David's story is told as a model of strength joined to repentance. The surah treats the denial of resurrection as the root of careless living. Pride is treated as the root of rejection, not a lack of evidence.

phrases.translation: Or should We treat the righteous like the wicked
phrases.explanation: The second question repeats the point with different words, making the distinction between the righteous and the wicked the basis of the judgment to come. The chapter links his worship to the praise of the mountains and birds. The chapter links the fate of individuals to the communities they trusted.

phrases.translation: ˹This is˺ a blessed Book which We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ so that they may contemplate its verses,
phrases.explanation: The Quran is called blessed and is given so that people reflect on its verses, not merely recite them, since reflection is the purpose of revelation. His kingship is described through justice, wisdom, and decisive judgment. The text repeatedly contrasts those who reflect with those who dismiss.

phrases.translation: and people of reason may be mindful
phrases.explanation: Those who use their reason are the ones meant to take heed, so understanding and remembrance are joined rather than separated. The story of the two plaintiffs is told as a test rather than as a legal report alone. The prophets are honoured for turning back to God, not for never making a mistake.

phrases.translation: And We blessed David with Solomon—what an excellent servant ˹he was˺!
phrases.explanation: Solomon is given to David as a son and is called an excellent servant, a description rooted in obedience and abundant remembrance of God. His prayer is read as a request for a sign of prophethood rather than for worldly greed. The surah treats the natural world as a sign of the Creator's power, not as a rival to it.

phrases.translation: Indeed, he ˹constantly˺ turned ˹to Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The word for constantly turning back is explained as returning to God from what He dislikes, as frequent glorification, or as abundant obedience, with all of those meanings preserved. The subjected wind and jinn show creation serving a prophet by God's command. The text treats the unseen world as real without inviting speculation beyond what is told.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when the well-trained, swift horses were paraded before him in the evening
phrases.explanation: The horses are described as trained and swift, standing on the tips of their hooves, and one report says there were twenty of them with wings, displayed to him in the evening. The gift is described as free of reckoning, though its exact scope was debated. The text honours those who remain faithful when their neighbours mock them.

phrases.translation: He then proclaimed, “I am truly in love with ˹these˺ fine things out of remembrance for Allah,”
phrases.explanation: His love for the horses is linked to the remembrance of God, though the reports also connect his preoccupation with them to a prayer that was missed. The passage ends, as David's did, with nearness to God and a good final home. Its accounts of Paradise and Hell give moral weight to ordinary decisions.

phrases.translation: until they went out of sight
phrases.explanation: The phrase is often read as the horses disappearing from view, and some early accounts take it as the sun setting, which explains the loss of the prayer. The story keeps power and humility together instead of treating them as opposites. Its warnings are never separated from the possibility of forgiveness.

phrases.translation: ˹He ordered,˺ “Bring them back to me!”
phrases.explanation: He calls for the horses to be returned to him, an order that leads to a gesture whose meaning was debated among early readers. The chapter uses Solomon's kingdom to point back to the Giver of every bounty. The chapter treats the whole world as the audience of one reminder.

phrases.translation: Then he began to rub down their legs and necks
phrases.explanation: Some took the rubbing as cutting their hamstrings and necks, while others took it as stroking them out of affection, and the latter view is preferred because a prophet would not harm an animal without cause. Solomon is introduced as an excellent servant who constantly turned back to God. The surah keeps returning to the Quran as a reminder that people are responsible to weigh.

phrases.translation: And indeed, We tested Solomon, placing a ˹deformed˺ body on his throne,
phrases.explanation: The test is described as a body cast upon his throne, and reports explain it as a devil who took human form and sat in his place, with several names given for that being. The horses, the wind, and the jinn all mark a kingdom given rather than seized. Its questions are designed to be answered by the listeners themselves.

phrases.translation: then he turned ˹to Allah in repentance˺
phrases.explanation: Solomon's response is to turn back to God, so the loss of his throne becomes an occasion for repentance rather than only a story of power. The chapter treats his authority as a gift that followed repentance. The surah treats patience as the Prophet's task while God handles the outcome.

phrases.translation: He prayed, “My Lord! Forgive me, and grant me an authority that will never be matched by anyone after me.
phrases.explanation: He asks for forgiveness and for a kingdom no one after him will match, which the reports read as a sign of his prophethood, an honour, or a rule that will not be taken from him again. The reports differ over the details of the horses and the body on his throne. Its scenes of judgment reverse the worldly status people trusted in.

phrases.translation: You are indeed the Giver ˹of all bounties˺.”
phrases.explanation: The prayer closes by naming God as the Giver, acknowledging that the kingdom he asks for is a gift rather than something he can seize. His prayer is read as a request for a sign of prophethood rather than for worldly greed. The stories show that honour with God can survive a serious error.

phrases.translation: So We subjected to him the wind, blowing gently at his command to wherever he pleased
phrases.explanation: The wind is made gentle and obedient to Solomon, moving at his command to whatever place he intended, which the reports describe as a wind submissive to him. The subjected wind and jinn show creation serving a prophet by God's command. The surah asks readers to see their own choices in the stories of earlier peoples.

phrases.translation: And ˹We subjected to him˺ every builder and diver of the jinn
phrases.explanation: The jinn are placed at his service as builders and divers, and the reports describe them as devils subjected to him for work no human could do. The gift is described as free of reckoning, though its exact scope was debated. Its closing words give the argument back to the One who sent the reminder.

phrases.translation: and others bound together in chains
phrases.explanation: Others among them are described as bound in fetters, showing that his authority included restraint as well as employment of those beings. The passage ends, as David's did, with nearness to God and a good final home. Its portraits of kingship stress service rather than privilege.

phrases.translation: ˹Allah said,˺ “This is Our gift, so give or withhold ˹as you wish˺, never to be called to account.”
phrases.explanation: The grant is called a gift without reckoning, and the reports differ over what may be given or withheld, whether the subjected jinn, their release from chains, or the free use of what God bestowed. The story keeps power and humility together instead of treating them as opposites. The text treats the abuse of authority as a failure of judgment with lasting effects.

phrases.translation: And he will indeed have ˹a status of˺ closeness to Us and an honourable destination
phrases.explanation: As with David, the story ends with nearness to God and a good final home, so the account of Solomon's kingdom closes on his standing with his Lord. The chapter uses Solomon's kingdom to point back to the Giver of every bounty. Pride is treated as the root of rejection, not a lack of evidence.

phrases.translation: And remember Our servant Job,
phrases.explanation: Job is introduced as God's servant, and his story is told as an example of patience under affliction rather than as a complaint against God. The reports explain the difficult words of the story while preserving its moral point. The text leaves room for uncertainty where the reports differ, rather than forcing one view.

phrases.translation: when he cried out to his Lord, “Satan has afflicted me with distress and suffering.”
phrases.explanation: He names Satan as the source of his distress and suffering, words the reports explain as trial, torment, and evil, while he still turns to his Lord for relief. His story connects suffering, prayer, and relief in a short space. Its warnings are addressed to people who already had access to guidance.

phrases.translation: ˹We responded,˺ “Stomp your foot: ˹now˺ here is a cool ˹and refreshing˺ spring for washing and drinking.”
phrases.explanation: He is told to strike the ground with his foot, and reports say one spring gushed for washing and another for drinking, cool water that answered both his need and his thirst. Job's story is told as the clearest example of patience in the surah. The chapter values a warning delivered plainly over a claim to special status.

phrases.translation: And We gave him back his family, twice as many,
phrases.explanation: His family is restored to him doubled, so his loss is not merely replaced but exceeded by God's mercy. His cry to God names affliction without accusing God of injustice. The surah treats the Day of Reckoning as the answer to a creation without purpose. The stories move quickly, but each one leaves a clear moral point.

phrases.translation: as a mercy from Us and a lesson for people of reason
phrases.explanation: The restoration is described as mercy from God and a lesson for those who reflect, since the story teaches how patience is rewarded. The cool spring answers both his need for washing and his thirst. The chapter shows that power belongs to God even when His servants appear weak.

phrases.translation: ˹And We said to him,˺ “Take in your hand a bundle of grass, and strike ˹your wife˺ with it, and do not break your oath.”
phrases.explanation: A bundle of grass means a handful of stems or branches, and one report says he struck once with a branch of a hundred twigs, keeping an oath without harming his wife. The restoration of his family is described as mercy doubled rather than merely returned. The surah keeps joining belief in one God with the way a person judges and acts.

phrases.translation: We truly found him patient. What an excellent servant ˹he was˺!
phrases.explanation: God's verdict is that Job was patient, and he is called an excellent servant, so the story defines patience as endurance that still turns to God. The bundle of grass shows an oath kept without harming the person he loved. Its final promise leaves the timing with God and the response with the listener.

phrases.translation: Indeed, he ˹constantly˺ turned ˹to Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The closing description of him as constantly turning back to God links Job with David and Solomon, whose stories used the same phrase. The chapter calls him patient and an excellent servant who turned back to God. The surah asks its readers to measure their deeds against what God has revealed.

phrases.translation: And remember Our servants: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—the men of strength and insight
phrases.explanation: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are called servants marked by strength and insight, and the reports note both a singular and a plural reading of the phrase while treating both as sound. The passage links the prophets of the past to the warning given to the Meccans. The surah treats revelation as a gift that no community can claim to control.

phrases.translation: We truly chose them for the honour of proclaiming the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: Their distinction is connected to the Hereafter, explained as reminding people of it, working for it, or being given its best reward, with the reports preserving these different readings. The section closes by promising an honourable destination for the righteous. Its descriptions of the next life are meant to shape decisions in this one.

phrases.translation: And in Our sight they are truly among the chosen and the finest
phrases.explanation: They are described as chosen and excellent in God's sight, so their honour rests on His estimation rather than on public recognition. The chapter gathers several prophets into one short list of remembrance. The chapter makes responsibility personal even when error was shared. Its language of tasting, seeing, and knowing makes the consequences concrete.

phrases.translation: Also remember Ishmael, Elisha, and Ⱬul-Kifl.
phrases.explanation: Ishmael, Elisha, and Dhul-Kifl are added to the list, and the Prophet is told to follow their example in patience and in conveying the message. They are marked by strength, insight, and a concern for the Hereafter. The surah treats mercy and justice as working together rather than against each other.

phrases.translation: All are among the best
phrases.explanation: All of them are counted among the best, and the word in Dhul-Kifl is explained as meaning a portion or a share of good fortune. The reports preserve variant readings of these names and phrases as equally sound. The chapter presents the Quran as blessing and warning at the same time.

phrases.translation: This is ˹all˺ a reminder.
phrases.explanation: The surah calls the preceding accounts a reminder, so the stories of the prophets are meant to prompt reflection rather than simply preserve history. The Prophet is told to follow their example in patience and in conveying the message. The text insists that turning away from a message is a choice with a cost.

phrases.translation: And the righteous will certainly have an honourable destination
phrases.explanation: The reminder ends with a promise that the God-fearing will have a good final home, which the following verses begin to describe. Their honour is said to lie in God's sight rather than in public praise. The chapter shows that those who lead others astray do not escape what follows.

phrases.translation: the Gardens of Eternity, whose gates will be open for them
phrases.explanation: Their destination is the Gardens of Eden, and the gates are described as opened for them, a welcome rather than a barrier at the entrance. The chapter contrasts lasting provision with worldly goods that perish. Its contrasts are meant to be weighed, not merely admired. The chapter holds power and repentance together in its portraits of the prophets.

phrases.translation: There they will recline, calling for abundant fruit and drink
phrases.explanation: They recline on couches and call for plentiful fruit and drink, an image of ease in which every request is answered. The descriptions are meant to shape choices before the Day of Reckoning. The chapter joins a warning about judgment to an invitation to turn back.

phrases.translation: And with them will be maidens of modest gaze and equal age
phrases.explanation: Companions of restrained gaze and matching age are part of that reward, and the reports note differences over the details while keeping the description of dignity and harmony. The passage gives the positive side of the distinction made earlier in the surah. Every narrative in the surah points back to the oneness of God and the certainty of judgment.

phrases.translation: This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning
phrases.explanation: The blessing is tied to the Day of Reckoning, so it is the promised outcome of judgment rather than a reward already earned in this life. The reward of the righteous is described as a home with open gates. The chapter shows that delay in punishment is not the same as safety.

phrases.translation: This is indeed Our provision that will never end
phrases.explanation: The provision never runs out, because each fruit that is plucked is replaced by another, unlike worldly goods that perish through consumption and decay. The scene of reclining and calling for fruit answers the warnings of the previous section. Gratitude appears as the proper response to a gift no one could earn.

phrases.translation: That is that. And the transgressors will certainly have the worst destination
phrases.explanation: The surah turns from the reward of the God-fearing to the transgressors, those who set themselves against their Lord, and says their final home will be the worst. The section turns from the reward of the righteous to the fate of the transgressors. Its questions about who controls mercy expose the limits of human authority.

phrases.translation: Hell, where they will burn. What an evil place to rest
phrases.explanation: That home is Hell, where they burn, and it is called an evil resting place because it is the bed they prepared for themselves by their own deeds. Hell is described as an evil resting place prepared by the deeds of its people. The text treats every messenger's rejection as part of one long history.

phrases.translation: Let them then taste this: boiling water and ˹oozing˺ pus
phrases.explanation: They are told to taste boiling water and a festering fluid, which the reports describe as pus and blood from their skins, as a spring of gathered venom, or as unbearable cold, leaving the exact nature uncertain. The reports differ over the exact nature of the boiling water and festering fluid. The stories move quickly, but each one leaves a clear moral point.

phrases.translation: and other torments of the same sort
phrases.explanation: Further punishments of similar kinds are added, and the reports mention paired torments including bitter cold, so the suffering is varied rather than a single pain. The people of the Fire are shown blaming one another rather than themselves. The text gives space to doubt so that it can be answered rather than hidden.

phrases.translation: ˹The misleaders will say to one another,˺ “Here is a crowd ˹of followers˺ being thrown in with us.
phrases.explanation: The leaders in the Fire see a crowd of followers driven in with them, and the phrase of welcome is denied to those who arrive. The leaders and followers exchange curses and each side asks for more punishment on the other. Its closing reminder answers the opening oath by the same Quran.

phrases.translation: They are not welcome, ˹for˺ they ˹too˺ will burn in the Fire.”
phrases.explanation: They say the newcomers will burn as well, so the leaders' greeting is a curse rather than comfort, and shared punishment produces shared hostility. The tyrants look for the believers they had despised and cannot find them. The fate of earlier peoples is offered as a pattern the present deniers are repeating.

phrases.translation: The followers will respond, “No! You are not welcome! You brought this upon us. What an evil place for settlement!”
phrases.explanation: The followers return the rejection and blame the leaders for leading them there, calling the Fire an evil settlement, so each side holds the other responsible. The chapter insists that this dispute is a certain truth, not an invented story. The chapter treats justice in judgment as a duty laid on those who hold authority.

phrases.translation: Adding, “Our Lord! Whoever brought this upon us, double their punishment in the Fire.”
phrases.explanation: They ask God to double the punishment of those who prepared this for them, meaning the leaders who called them in the world to the deeds that earned the Fire. The passage shows worldly status reversed when judgment comes. The text insists that inherited practice is not proof of truth.

phrases.translation: The tyrants will ask ˹one another˺, “But why do we not see those we considered to be lowly
phrases.explanation: The tyrants look for people they had counted among the worst, the poor believers they had despised in the world, and wonder why they are not in the Fire with them. The section treats shared error as something that does not remove personal responsibility. Its repeated command to remember makes reflection a duty, not a hobby.

phrases.translation: Were we wrong in mocking them ˹in the world˺?
phrases.explanation: They ask whether their mockery of those believers was mistaken, and the word for mockery also carries the meaning of taking people into service and humiliating them. The dispute is reported as a fact about the next life rather than a warning about this one alone. Its language of tasting, seeing, and knowing makes the consequences concrete.

phrases.translation: Or do our eyes ˹just˺ fail to see them ˹in the Fire˺?”
phrases.explanation: They wonder whether their eyes have missed the believers who might be with them in the Fire, a question that shows how completely their worldly judgments have been overturned. The section turns from the reward of the righteous to the fate of the transgressors. The surah treats the hastening of punishment as a reckless request, not courage.

phrases.translation: This dispute between the residents of the Fire will certainly come to pass
phrases.explanation: The surah insists that this mutual reproaching, cursing, and pleading among the people of the Fire is certain truth, not a story invented to frighten. Hell is described as an evil resting place prepared by the deeds of its people. The text treats a prophet's honesty as central to the message he brings.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I am only a warner.
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to say that his role is only to warn of a severe punishment, urging people to guard against it by repentance rather than to force belief. The section returns to the themes of the opening verses with a direct command to speak. The surah honours obedience that does not wait for a guaranteed outcome.

phrases.translation: And there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Allah—the One, the Supreme
phrases.explanation: The confession of faith names the One who has no partner or consort and who overpowers everything beneath Him, rather than the powerless idols they served. The divine titles join power and forgiveness in one description. Its stories are told as signs for the listener, not only as records of the past.

phrases.translation: ˹He is the˺ Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between—the Almighty, Most Forgiving.”
phrases.explanation: The same God is Lord of all that lies between heaven and earth, mighty in power and forgiving to those who turn back, so warning and mercy are held together. The Prophet is told to define his role plainly as a warner. The chapter holds power and repentance together in its portraits of the prophets.

phrases.translation: Say, “This ˹Quran˺ is momentous news
phrases.explanation: The Quran is called a tremendous tiding, and the reports identify that tiding with the Quran itself and with the judgment it announces. The confession of God's oneness is joined to the warning of punishment. The stories of David, Solomon, and Job share a single phrase about turning back to God.

phrases.translation: from which you ˹pagans˺ are turning away.”
phrases.explanation: The charge is that they turn away from that news, so their problem is not ignorance of a message but avoidance of one they have heard. The Quran is called momentous news from which the pagans turn away. The surah presents prophecy as one message delivered by many servants.

phrases.translation: ˹And say,˺ “I had no knowledge of the highest assembly ˹in heaven˺ when they differed ˹concerning Adam˺
phrases.explanation: The Prophet says he had no knowledge of the angels' dispute about Adam except through revelation, so his account of unseen matters is not a guess or a borrowed story. The chapter stresses that his knowledge of unseen matters came only through revelation. The chapter uses the failure of Iblis to show where pride leads.

phrases.translation: What is revealed to me is that I am only sent with a clear warning.”
phrases.explanation: What is revealed to him is only the warning, and he is a warner who brings clarity, a role that limits his claim while making the message plain. The warning is clear, so the listeners cannot claim they were not told. Its arguments move from the visible world to truths that cannot be seen.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember, O Prophet˺ when your Lord said to the angels, “I am going to create a human being from clay
phrases.explanation: The narrative of Adam begins with God telling the angels that He will create a human being from clay, an announcement made before the creature exists. The narrative shows that obedience to God's command is the test of every creature. The chapter treats reflection on the Quran as the purpose of its revelation.

phrases.translation: So when I have fashioned him and had a spirit of My Own ˹creation˺ breathed into him,
phrases.explanation: The command follows the completion of his form and the breathing of a spirit into him, which the reports explain as God's power rather than a part of God. The story of Adam is told to explain the origin of Iblis's hostility. The surah treats the denial of resurrection as the root of careless living.

phrases.translation: fall down in prostration to him.”
phrases.explanation: The angels are told to bow down before the finished human being, an honour that becomes the test of their obedience and the occasion of Iblis's refusal. The angels are commanded to prostrate to a human being formed from clay. The chapter links the fate of individuals to the communities they trusted.

phrases.translation: So the angels prostrated all together—
phrases.explanation: All the angels prostrate together, so the command is obeyed without exception among them, which sharpens the contrast with the one who refused. The breathing of the spirit is explained as God's power, not as a part of God. The text repeatedly contrasts those who reflect with those who dismiss.

phrases.translation: but not Iblîs, who acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful
phrases.explanation: Iblis is the exception, and his refusal is described as arrogance that made him unfaithful, so the failure is moral rather than intellectual. The refusal of Iblis is traced to pride rather than to a lack of knowledge. The prophets are honoured for turning back to God, not for never making a mistake.

phrases.translation: Allah asked, “O Iblîs! What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My Own Hands?
phrases.explanation: God questions Iblis about refusing to bow to a being He created with His own hands, and reports list the Throne, Eden, the Pen, and Adam among the things made directly by His hand. The argument from fire and clay ignores the honour God gave to Adam. The surah treats the natural world as a sign of the Creator's power, not as a rival to it.

phrases.translation: Did you ˹just˺ become proud? Or have you always been arrogant?”
phrases.explanation: The question asks whether his pride was new or long-standing, exposing an arrogance that had been present before the command was given. The curse and the respite set limits on the tempter's power. The text treats the unseen world as real without inviting speculation beyond what is told.

phrases.translation: He replied, “I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay.”
phrases.explanation: Iblis argues from his origin, claiming that fire is superior to clay, a comparison of materials that ignores the honour God gave the human being. Satan's own words except God's chosen servants from his threat. The text honours those who remain faithful when their neighbours mock them.

phrases.translation: Allah commanded, “Then get out of Paradise, for you are truly cursed
phrases.explanation: He is expelled from Paradise and declared accursed, so the refusal to bow ends in exclusion from the place of honour. The chapter ends the encounter with a settled judgment about Hell. Its accounts of Paradise and Hell give moral weight to ordinary decisions. Its final promise leaves the timing with God and the response with the listener.

phrases.translation: And surely upon you is My condemnation until the Day of Judgment.”
phrases.explanation: The curse is said to remain upon him until the Day of Judgment, which gives his hostility a fixed limit rather than an unlimited power. The reports preserve variant readings of the truth saying while keeping both meanings sound. Its warnings are never separated from the possibility of forgiveness.

phrases.translation: Satan appealed, “My Lord! Then delay my end until the Day of their resurrection.”
phrases.explanation: Satan asks to be spared until the day people are raised, a request for time rather than forgiveness, so his concern is with the opportunity to tempt. The narrative shows that obedience to God's command is the test of every creature. The chapter treats the whole world as the audience of one reminder.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “You will be delayed
phrases.explanation: God grants the delay, so the respite he asks for is given, though it remains bounded by the term that follows. The story of Adam is told to explain the origin of Iblis's hostility. The surah keeps returning to the Quran as a reminder that people are responsible to weigh.

phrases.translation: until the appointed Day.”
phrases.explanation: The delay lasts only until a day already appointed, so his power over people is permitted for a time and not left to run without limit. The angels are commanded to prostrate to a human being formed from clay. Its questions are designed to be answered by the listeners themselves.

phrases.translation: Satan said, “By Your Glory! I will certainly mislead them all
phrases.explanation: Satan swears by God's glory that he will lead all of them astray, a boast that claims a reach wider than the authority he has been given. The breathing of the spirit is explained as God's power, not as a part of God. The surah treats patience as the Prophet's task while God handles the outcome.

phrases.translation: except Your chosen servants among them.”
phrases.explanation: He excepts God's chosen servants, admitting that those whom God has purified remain beyond his reach, which limits his threat from his own mouth. The refusal of Iblis is traced to pride rather than to a lack of knowledge. Its scenes of judgment reverse the worldly status people trusted in.

phrases.translation: Allah concluded, “The truth is—and I ˹only˺ say the truth—
phrases.explanation: God answers with a statement about truth, and two well-known readings of the phrase are both treated as sound, one taking it as a declaration that He is the truth and speaks the truth. The argument from fire and clay ignores the honour God gave to Adam. The stories show that honour with God can survive a serious error.

phrases.translation: I will surely fill up Hell with you
phrases.explanation: The declared outcome is that Hell will be filled with Iblis, a judgment stated as settled rather than as a possibility. The curse and the respite set limits on the tempter's power. The surah asks readers to see their own choices in the stories of earlier peoples.

phrases.translation: and whoever follows you from among them, all together.”
phrases.explanation: Those who follow him are included with him, so the fate of the tempter and the tempted is shared, and both readings of the opening phrase keep that meaning. Satan's own words except God's chosen servants from his threat. Its closing words give the argument back to the One who sent the reminder.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹Quran˺,
phrases.explanation: The Prophet asks for no payment for conveying the Quran, which removes any suspicion that he invented the message for personal gain. The final verses define the Quran as a reminder for all peoples. Its portraits of kingship stress service rather than privilege. The chapter joins a warning about judgment to an invitation to turn back.

phrases.translation: nor do I pretend to be someone I am not
phrases.explanation: He also disclaims any pretence, so his role is limited to delivering what he was given rather than claiming a status he was not granted. The last warning leaves the timing of its fulfilment indefinite. The text treats the abuse of authority as a failure of judgment with lasting effects.

phrases.translation: It is only a reminder to the whole world
phrases.explanation: The Quran is described as nothing but a reminder for all peoples, a message whose scope is universal rather than limited to one tribe or generation. The reports differ over when the promised knowledge will come, so the chapter does not fix a date. Pride is treated as the root of rejection, not a lack of evidence.

phrases.translation: And you will certainly know its truth before long.”
phrases.explanation: The surah ends by saying they will know the truth of the message after a time, and since the reports differ over whether that means death, Badr, or the Resurrection, the safest reading leaves the timing indefinite as God left it. The closing words return to the Quran with which the surah began. The text leaves room for uncertainty where the reports differ, rather than forcing one view.
